referents.why: 'Me' is Pharaoh, the speaker of the words, not the speaker of the narrative.
referents.category: first person of the speaker's words

referents.why: 'My people' are Pharaoh's people, in his own words.
referents.category: first person of the speaker's words

referents.why: 'He said' is Pharaoh, named as subject of the summoning in cl0.
'Pray' is a plural imperative addressed to the two summoned, Moses and Aaron, taken as one composite.
'That he may remove the frogs' asks the LORD; the third-person jussive has the LORD as its subject, and the LORD is named in this verse.
referents.category: referent of a request to God

referents.why: 'I will let go' is Pharaoh's own promise (first person singular cohortative).
referents.category: first person of the speaker's words

referents.why: 'That they may sacrifice' is third masculine plural, and the people let go are the collective 'people' (your people), which takes plural agreement.
referents.category: plural agreement with a collective noun

links.why: Reversed: the summoning (cl0) comes before the saying (cl1). The forward link cl0 then cl1 is kept.
The wayyiqtol 'he said' continues after 'he summoned'.
A command joined by waw to a jussive of a different person is read as so that.
'Pray, so that he may remove the frogs': the jussive is the aim of the prayer.
The promise follows the removal in sequence. There is no purpose or cause marker, and no 'if' stands, so the plain waw is kept. See cant_tell.
A waw joins a cohortative (letting go) to a jussive of a different person, which the and-rule reads as so that.
'I will let the people go, so that they may sacrifice to the LORD.'
'He said' introduces the speech whose content is the command 'pray' with its aim.

groups.why: Pharaoh's words to Moses and Aaron: a command with its aim, then his own promise and the purpose of it.
'Pray' is the command; 'that he may remove the frogs' is its aim, a third-person jussive that commands no one.
'That he may remove' is an aim, not a command. The builder's imp3 duplicates the aim and takes the promise as a part.
The cohortative is a promise, not a command. Its relation to cl5 is carried by the purpose link.

cant_tell.what: Whether 'I will let your people go' (cl4) may be the source of a purpose link, since the purpose type is written with a command as its source.
cant_tell.why: The cohortative is a promise, and the form allows either reading. The purpose link is recorded because the sense requires it, and it is flagged here.

cant_tell.what: Whether Pharaoh's promise (cl4) is conditional on the removal of the frogs (cl3).
cant_tell.why: 'Then I will let go' follows the removal with no 'if'. The link types have no bare conditional without a marker, so the plain and is kept.
